title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 309: The Pyrocene: Fire, Humans, and the Shaping of Earth
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 309 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Pyrocene: Fire, Humans, and the Shaping of Earth

Paragraph 1. For more than a century, western forestry rules treated fire as an unnatural disaster that had to be stopped at every cost. Famous campaigns warned the public that wildfires ruined timber and damaged wild parks. Yet in Fire: A Brief History, environmental historian Stephen Pyne argues that total fire suppression was a serious ecological mistake. Rather than being an outside enemy, fire has shaped land ecosystems for millions of years and served as humanity's oldest environmental tool.

Paragraph 2. Our partnership with fire began long before modern humans appeared. Early ancestors learned how to capture and control flames to cook tough roots and meat. Cooking softened hard foods, sharply lowering the bodily energy spent on chewing and digesting meals. This extra energy fuelled the rapid growth of human brains, while human jaws and digestive systems gradually shrank.

Paragraph 3. Fire also became the earliest tool for managing landscapes. Indigenous communities across Australia, North America, and southern Africa practised careful cultural burning. Rather than letting dead plants pile up endlessly, they started gentle, low-heat fires that cleared thick undergrowth, encouraged special fire-loving seeds to sprout, and kept fields open for grazing animals. Because dry fuel was burned away regularly, huge uncontrollable fires were extremely rare. In truth, the lands European explorers admired as untouched wilderness had been carefully managed by native fires for thousands of years.

Paragraph 4. Trouble began when colonial governments and modern foresters banned traditional native burning during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Officials believed removing all flames would protect valuable wooden forests for commercial logging. Instead, stopping every small blaze created what Pyne calls the 'pyric paradox': enormous piles of dead branches and dry leaves built up silently on forest floors.

Paragraph 5. Today, these unnaturally crowded forests combine with global warming to produce terrifying firestorms. Modern super-fires burn with such extreme heat that they bake the ground, kill underground seedbanks, and permanently change local nature. After fighting small fires for a century, modern society now faces an age of unmanageable flames.

q1.text: For over a hundred years, western forestry policy tried to stop all forest fires.

steps: Đoạn 1: "...treated fire as an unnatural disaster that had to be stopped at every cost."

q2.text: Cooking raw food caused early human jaws and stomachs to grow larger.

steps: Đoạn 2: Chỉ có não lớn lên, còn hàm và hệ tiêu hóa thu nhỏ lại (gradually shrank).

q3.text: Commercial logging companies trained native workers to light controlled fires.

steps: Đoạn 4: Có nhắc gỗ thương mại (commercial logging) nhưng không nói công ty gỗ đào tạo người bản địa đốt rừng.

q4.text: Rising global temperatures today help make forest firestorms more severe.

steps: Đoạn 5: Rừng rậm tích tụ nhiên liệu kết hợp với nóng lên toàn cầu (global warming) tạo ra bão lửa khủng khiếp.

q5.text: Plant seeds hidden underground always survive modern super-fires without damage.

steps: Đoạn 5: Siêu cháy rừng đốt chết cả ngân hàng hạt giống dưới đất (kill underground seedbanks).
